#3279. Gentler Streak 6.0 adds a new wellbeing timeline and customizable dashboard

In an update rolling out today, Gentler Streak is introducing new ways for users to track their wellbeing and personalize the app’s guidance based on how they feel. Here are the details.

One of my favorite exercise-tracking apps got even better today with an update that expands its functionality beyond workouts and fitness metrics to better reflect how users actually feel.

Starting today, Gentler Streak will let users log how they feel each day, including their mood, symptoms, and other factors that may not be reflected in their health and fitness data.

Some days, the way we feel isn’t reflected in what the data says, no matter the data quality. “How I Feel” captures the part that devices can’t grasp: personal context. And how you feel is not only a mood: it is also a sore throat, heavy legs or a poor night’s sleep. The feature was inspired by the Gentler Streak community, including people living with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia, ADHD, and those not wearing their Apple Watch at night. Without overnight signals, their guidance has less to work with.

According to the team behind Gentler Streak, these new features are aimed at users whose health and fitness data may not accurately reflect how they feel, including those dealing with chronic conditions, menopause, stress, or poor sleep.

In practice, the app will now feature four tabs: Today, Health, Workouts, and Insights. In the Today and Health tabs, a new “Anything to add?” field will let users rate how they feel, from Great to Off, and add context about what might be affecting their well-being, including fatigue, feeling calm, or custom tags.

You decide when the prompt appears. Go to Profile > Settings > Self-Evaluation Prompt and choose one of three options: only when your vitals or sleep are off, always on, or never.

Gentler Stories notes that the self-assessments will override the app’s wellbeing estimates for that day, with its daily guidance adjusting accordingly.

The Today tab will also feature an expanded 10- or 30-day timeline showing logged workouts, wellbeing estimates, potential symptoms, poor sleep or vitals, and the first day of a menstrual period, while Health will introduce an interactive chart showing users how their wellbeing changes over time, with the ability to filter by symptoms.

Users can now also customize which information appears on their Today screen, including vitals, sleep, steps, menstrual cycle, VO₂ max, and workouts, which is a nice touch.

For users who are sick, injured, or taking a break from exercise, the app’s hallmark Activity Path will make way for a new Wellbeing Path, which lets them track their wellbeing on a daily basis.

For users with Active status, a new colorful wellbeing line will appear beneath the Activity Path, reflecting how they feel each day. This information is logged automatically for those who wear their Apple Watch overnight, or based on self-assessments for those who don’t.

Importantly, Gentler Stories notes that all information entered through the new feature remains on the user’s device, with no accounts or company-operated servers involved.

Gentler Streak is available for free on the App Store, with in-app purchases for monthly, yearly, family, and lifetime subscriptions.

A thoughtful gift doesn’t have to be an expensive one, but there’s nothing wrong with splurging a little for someone you care about. A quality gift for a loved one (or even yourself) can be a special way to add a little magic year-round.

Whether you’re shopping for someone who appreciates the finer things, or you just want an extra-special way to show you care, we’ve rounded up the best luxury gifts you can buy online. These are also gifts that go beyond the usual flowers and chocolates, to show that you’re selecting something based on your recipient’s taste and personality.

The latest Sony headphones are also the best headphones the legendary audio company has ever released, thanks to a bespoke driver tuned by Grammy-winning engineers, incredible noise canceling that you can feel as soon as you put the earpads on, and a 360 Reality Audio Upmix feature, which automatically elevates what you’re listening to into an immersive surround sound-style experience.But what truly makes these headphones luxurious is their sleek and sculpted design, with supple vegan leather and bold metallic accents combining to create a piece that looks as good as it sounds.

Choose from a wide variety of colors, prints, patterns and silhouettes, and have your dream suit sewn to your specifications. This is a great gift for a special occasion (like a wedding or anniversary), but also an opportunity to gift the men in your life a go-to suit for galas, cocktail functions or an everyday suit for work. SuitShop says their made-to-order model is also more sustainable than buying premade suit sets online — with SuitShop, you make exactly what you want and only what you want, ensuring there is no waste from overproduction.

Polo Ralph Lauren’s bear sweater is an iconic gift for the preppy type. There are so many options of bears to choose from, from the Tweed Bear to the Painter Bear (and even this bow tie bear seen here), making the sweater something of a collectible. Macy’s has styles and sizes for both men and women available here.

Coach’s Chelsea Shoulder Bag went viral in 2026 and for all the right reasons: its slouchy shape, supple leather construction and minimalist design make this unisex bag a fit for basically anything and anyone. Pack the bag for work, for example, or use it as your airplane personal item when traveling. A large interior capacity and a zip pocket make organization easy, while the adjustable strap lets you sling this over your shoulder or wear it as a messenger.

Sandy Liang does coquette better than anyone and the Recital bag is the perfect gift for someone who loves all things cutesy, but doesn’t want something that’s too loud or kitschy. The understated bow detailing on the strap adds just the right touch of whimsy to an otherwise minimal bag, and the structure of the bag allows for it to transition from casual to formal occasions. It’s polished enough for a night out but also playful enough to be used as a daily bag. The Recital bag can fit right into any wardrobe as a great timeless accessory from season to season.

Dior’s luxurious creme gelée is designed to adapt to every skin type to deeply hydrate, visibly plump, and reveal a more radiant complexion. Made in France and inspired by caviar beads, It’s a self-care essential that makes a showstopping upgrade for anyone who takes skincare seriously. What we like: the formula is gentle enough for all skin types, while the beautifully-designed jar makes for a great #shelfie pic.

With a burn time of approximately 90 hours, you can’t go wrong with gifting this Le Labo candle in fan-favorite scent Santal 26. This concrete candle is a limited edition (with a special black version only available on Le Labo’s official site) and will last your gift recipient throughout the cold winter season. It’s a standout display piece for your home too, whether on a table or shelf.

This soft and cozy throw blanket adds an instant touch of elegance to your space, thanks to the artist-designed lion motif framed against sophisticated grey and stripes. Woven in Scotland from extra-fine Italian merino wool, the blanket measures 56 x 69 inches in size. It’s a gift that gives rich country manor vibes or heritage equestrian. It makes a great accent to your chaise or bed too.

Ariana Grande’s Swarovski capsule collection features sparkling music-inspired motifs, hearts, and pearls, making each piece the perfect add-on to an outfit to polish your look. The entire collection can be dressed up or down for any occasion and is a great gift idea for music fans and accessory collectors alike.This one seen here is made from rhodium-plated, heart-shaped crystals, but you can shop more picks — including bracelets, earrings and charms — at Swarovski.com.

Fragrances can be tricky to buy as gifts, but Baccarat Rouge 540 by Maison Francis Kurkdjian Paris widely beloved for a reason with a one-of-a-kind scent that’s both woody and floral, at once fresh and intense. The official olfactory notes include jasmine, saffron and moss, but it all combines into an intoxicating scent that’s instantly memorably but virtually untraceable. In other words, you’ll have everyone coming up to you to ask, “What are you wearing?”

This classic shoe from Maison Margiela, inspired by the 1970s, has stood the test of time and is a great sneaker staple for anyone’s collection. They are stylish but also comfortable and can be dressed up or down, making them truly versatile. While Black and White are classic colors, a handful of fun colors like Cloud and Boero have been added to the lineup if you’re looking for a pop. For sneakerheads on your gifting list, this is an easy way to elevate their footwear game.

Scarves are a gifting staple but think beyond basic plaid this year. Acne Studios scarves have become a stylish pick for fall and winter over the years and are an easy way to elevate an outfit without much effort. Crafted with an alpaca, wool and mohair blend, this scarf can be pulled out year after year while retaining incredible softness and warmth. It also comes in a few fun colorways that add a pop of color while still being simple enough to be paired with any look.

Few sports have taken off in recent years quite like F1, and this Formula 1 book from Assouline features luxe packaging and impressive photography tracing history-making moments on and off the track. The book is even scented with notes of rubber, making it a one-of-a-kind gift and an ultimate coffee table display piece.

Baies is a crowd-favorite scent from French fragrance house Diptyque and this hourglass diffuser makes a great gift because it combines form and function. It’s a stylish addition to any room and can keep your space smelling fresh and welcoming for guests, while offering an art-inspired alternative to burning a candle.

Balenciaga always finds a way to put its own stamp on luxury (pun intended), and this passport holder is no exception. A great luxury travel gift, the passport holder is also an unexpected gift for someone who is always on the go. There are four card slots and a flat pocket to keep you organized as you (hopefully) breeze through the airport with that other ultimate luxury: a first-class ticket.

#3276. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3275. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang set to be fired, with Johny Srouji among possible replacements [U]

Following reports of a potential second affair – this time with a subordinate – Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang looks certain to be fired by the company’s board, probably later today (though he may be allowed to ‘resign’). Apple’s chief hardware officer Johny Srouji has been listed among the potential replacements, though this seems unlikely.

Update: As we predicted, he’s gone today and Kress was indeed named interim CEO …

For anyone who’s been away from the planet for the past fortnight, Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy has been the main headline news in the tech press since it came to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days.

Things got even worse yesterday when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

It was already looking inevitable that he would be fired, and the latest revelation adds to the urgency. The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was meeting last night to discuss the CEO’s future. That future at Nvidia is likely to be measured in hours rather than days.

The board now needs to find a replacement, and Bloomberg provides a rundown on some of the potential candidates. CFO Colette Kress looks likely to head the list for at least an interim appointment. The paper names a number of other possibilities, including Apple’s chief hardware officer, Johny Srouji.

Srouji has led one of the most successful in-house silicon programs in the industry, overseeing the custom chips that power the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. His track record gives him deep credibility on chip design, product integration and long-term technology roadmaps. But much of his experience has been built inside Apple’s tightly controlled ecosystem, and he hasn’t been tested in the kind of high-profile salesmanship which Huang is famous for.

Given the urgency, my money is on Nvidia announcing Kress as at least interim CEO, if not a permanent replacement. It seems exceedingly unlikely that Srouji would be appointed at this time, given the in-depth negotiations and discussions that would need to take place.

As to whether he’s a potential candidate following an interim appointment, it still seems unlikely. There was an earlier report of his claimed dissatisfaction at the company, but it seems a stretch to imagine him jumping ship so soon after his promotion to chief hardware officer.

I finally get why people love traditional Zelda games so much

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2021, I wrote an op-ed titled “Breath of the Wild ruined traditional Zelda for me.” Back then, I mused that Breath of the Wild being my first-ever Zelda game had made going back to the older titles in the beloved Nintendo franchise difficult. Flash-forward to now, and I’m roughly halfway through the new Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Nintendo Switch 2, and I’m loving it.

I’ll cut my past self a little slack. February 2021 was more than five years ago, and a person’s tastes can change a lot in that amount of time. Heck, in those days, I also thought Souls games weren’t for me. Now in 2026, I’ve beaten every modern title FromSoftware has released (bar Dark Souls 2; it’s in my overflowing backlog) and am basically obsessed with the Soulslike genre.

Nevertheless, I definitely wrote off classic Zelda games too hastily. Turns out all it took was pretty much the most acclaimed video game of all time getting a stunning remake for me to see just how foolish I had been. Consider this follow-up article my formal apology to Link.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2, and in a word, it's stunning. This complete remake of the classic Nintendo 64 offers overhauled visuals, improved controls, and a few smart tweaks to make the timeless game even more modern. Ocarina of Time was considered a masterpiece back in 1998, and this new version on Switch 2 has earned the same plaudits.

Ocarina of Time starts a little slow. Lots of text boxes and simple tutorials. But once the adventure really begins, and Young Link is tasked with finding three Spiritual Stones (the first is obtained during the prologue chapter), I started to discover exactly why longtime fans bemoan Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom’s lack of “proper” Zelda dungeons.

But it was only once I had obtained all three stones and transformed into grown-up Link that I really understood what makes these dungeons so special, and why fans still beg for the series to bring them back. Nintendo’s penchant for creative and satisfying puzzles is on full display in the Forest, Fire and Water Temple, and I’m very excited to head to the remaining dungeons and discover what’s hiding within their twisting corridors.

The Fire Temple is a great example of phenomenal design, as the underground lava-laden cavern loops back on itself in surprising and creative ways. The infamous Water Temple might actually be my frontrunner favorite, probably because the remake has stripped away the friction of the original.

Best of all is the way each dungeon gives you a new tool to play with, which is then vital to unlocking the dungeon’s many secrets; it is a consistently brilliant way of asking players to make use of their entire arsenal of tools.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My favorite aspect of Breath of the Wild (and sequel Tears of the Kingdom) has always been the puzzle shrines. While it’s not an original opinion, the dungeons in Ocarina of Time feel like a couple dozen BOTW puzzle shrines stitched together in an environmentally cohesive manner.

Delving into a dungeon feels appropriately epic, and each one (or at least, each one I’ve experienced so far) begs to be fully explored with treasure chests and secrets for those willing to look in every corner. They’re just a blast, and yes, I can finally admit, they flow better than Breath of the Wild’s pretty repetitive Divine Beast dungeons.

While I’ve at long last come around to the strengths of the traditional Zelda formula, that doesn’t mean I’ve suddenly lost my intense love for Breath of the Wild and its own acclaimed formula. Sorry, Ocarina stans, but Link’s 2017 adventure remains my favorite game in the series (of the ones I’ve played).

If there is one element where Ocarina of Time can’t compete with Breath of the Wild, it’s in the latter's ability to let you solve puzzles in a multitude of ways. In Ocarina of Time, the tools at Link’s disposal are more rudimentary (understandable, it’s ultimately a remake of a game from 1998), typically giving players a singular way to progress. In Breath of the Wild (and especially Tears of the Kingdom), you can “break” puzzles in ingenious ways.

While playing modern Zelda, I’ve found myself looking up online guides, not even because I need help with a puzzle, but merely to see the different ways other players solved the various roadblocks in Link’s path. In Ocarina of Time, players will reach the exit in pretty much the same way.

But that's not necessarily to say there's no appeal to Ocarina of Time's more linear progression. As mentioned, the way tools like the hookshot are slowly dished out, giving you incentive to return to previous areas with a larger arsenal, is something that Breath of the Wild lacks. In that case, you get pretty much all your traversal and puzzle-solving abilities in the first area.

I think both classic and modern Zelda have huge strengths, and opting for one over the other in any future Zelda games would be disappointing. I hope the development team at Nintendo mashes the two design philosophies together. Imagine a Zelda game with an exploration-focused open Hyrule but also containing lengthy, tightly crafted dungeons? Best of both worlds.

Tears of the Kingdom was a step in this direction, but its dungeons still don’t compare to those in Ocarina of Time. So, I don’t know if what would now be my “dream” Zelda game will ever exist, and it’ll probably be a good few years now before Nintendo is ready to talk about the next mainline 3D game in the series. But I really hope Link’s next flagship adventure takes the best part of both traditional and modern Zelda games and satisfies fans of both camps.

A great example of blending the new and old is FromSoftware's Elden Ring, which offers a refreshing sense of freedom in its expansive overworld but also contains several "Legacy Dungeons." These are designed more like the smaller-scale areas found in the Dark Souls series. I hope that the Zelda team takes a similar approach when crafting whatever is next for the franchise.

In the meantime, I should probably circle back and give other classic Zelda games a chance, or maybe I’ll just keep my fingers crossed that the rumored Majora’s Mask remake materializes. I hear some fans consider it even better.

#3273. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3272. Why Apple shouldn’t worry about iPhone Duo returns

A poll of 9to5Mac readers who were lucky enough to take delivery of their iPhone Duo in the first few days shows that 30% of them have returned it for a refund.

While that could be considered bad news for the future of the device, I don’t personally consider it either surprising or worrying …

Following a report by The Verge on iPhone Duo buyers who opted to return the device for a refund within Apple’s 14-day “no questions asked” period, we thought it would be interesting to get a sense of how many people may have done this.

9to5Mac readers were always likely to have had their fingers hovering over the pre-order button for the best shot at taking early delivery, with the first of these having hit the end of the 14-day window. We ask those of you who fall into this category to tell us whether you kept or returned the device.

With close to 6,000 total votes, the results showed that close to a third of you returned your Duo.

For any other device, that would be a disastrous return rate. For the Duo, however, I don’t think it’s terribly surprising.

I voted to say I returned it just so I could see the results. I’ve never ordered nor returned an iPhone Duo.

Not providing a way to see the results without voting will have massively skewed the results. Even if the poll were better, this is a wild claim to draw from one specific, poorly assembled assembled poll.

As we noted yesterday, Apple described the iPhone Duo as “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original.” The size of that change shows up in a whole range of ways, from the weight of the device through the changed aspect ratio of the front display to a completely new way of using an iPhone.

Throw in the extremely high price tag, and I’ve always suspected that a significant number of iPhone Duo buyers would be viewing it as an experiment rather than a committed purchase. Our own Ryan Christoffel is an example of that “try it and see” attitude. One week in, he’s reached an interim conclusion that it’s probably not for him.

For those who’ve decided to return it, a number of readers shared their reasons.

“Returned it – I can’t go back to Touch ID.”

“I want to like it, but I just can’t get there. It’s awkward, and the outside screen is way too small.”

“Returned it. Not for me. I do not want to open the phone every time I want a larger screen and Apple made the outer display much less usable than it should be with that silly permanent dock. I also use my phones left-handed.”

“During a vacation in Morocco, we spent a night camping in the Sahara Desert. I was extremely careful with the phone and tried to avoid using it in the sand altogether. However, on the second day, when I opened it inside the tent, I heard a crunching sound coming from the hinge. Sand had somehow gotten inside. I tried everything I could to clean it, but nothing worked. The inner display was still functioning perfectly, but the phone would no longer open all the way. Even worse, when I tried to close it, I had to force it shut.”

For me personally, it couldn’t be my only phone, given the priority I place on the device as a camera, but I am still lusting after it. Given the continued extended delivery times – with random checks showing shipping in late January – I don’t think Apple has much to worry about here.

#3271. Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys’ Bass Singer, Dead at 83

Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist whose river-deep delivery of “oom poppa mow-mow” in the crossover hit “Elvira” helped give the Oak Ridge Boys their signature song, died Saturday. He was 83. Sterban’s rep, Jeremy Westby, confirmed the singer’s death, adding that the Country Music Hall of Fame member died “due to complications from bronchitis and pneumonia.” In March, Sterban said that he had been diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

A native of Collingswood, New Jersey, Sterban grew up across the Delaware River from his future Oak Ridge Boys bandmate, the Philadelphia-born Joe Bonsall. But the pair first crossed paths in the gospel music community, in the quartet the Keystones, which Sterban helped form.

Gospel music defined Sterban’s early years and put him in the circle of rock & roll royalty when he joined J.D. Sumner and the Stamps near the end of the Sixties and hit the road with the group behind Elvis Presley in 1971. Sterban toured with Presley until 1972 when he left to join the Oak Ridge Boys, but his time with “The King of Rock & Roll” was deeply impactful: In the 1972 doc Elvis on Tour, Sterban, fellow bass singer Sumner, and the Stamps are seen harmonizing backstage with Presley on the gospel standard “Bosom of Abraham.” He’d go on to detail his history with Presley in the 2012 memoir From Elvis to Elvira: My Life On Stage.

Prior to becoming country music stars, the Oak Ridge Boys — like both the Keystones and the Stamps — were primarily a gospel group. The outfit started as the Oak Ridge Quartet and cycled through numerous members before landing on the most well-known lineup of William Lee Golden, Duane Allen, Sterban, and Bonsall. In 1974, they released their self-titled album, but it was 1977’s Y’all Come Back Saloon and its title track that put them on the country music charts. (They were already on the radar of Paul Simon: In 1976, the songwriter recruited the Oaks to sing backup on his song “Slip Slidin’ Away.”) Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

A string of successful albums and singles followed — a version of Rodney Crowell’s “Leaving Louisiana in the Broad Daylight,” the Number One hit “Trying to Love Two Women” — leading up to the album that would turn them into radio hitmakers, 1981’s Fancy Free. The LP was a country music smash and went on to be certified double platinum, thanks to songs like the title track “(I’m Settin’) Fancy Free” and the crossover juggernaut “Elvira.”

Written by Dallas Frazier, “Elvira” — ranked No. 193 on Rolling Stone‘s list of the 200 Greatest Country Songs of All Time — became a country Number One hit and peaked at Number Five on the pop charts. It also won the Oaks a Grammy in 1982 for Best Country Performance by a Duo or Group With Vocal, and was named Single of the Year by both the Country Music Association and Academy of Country Music. It was a testament to Sterban’s dramatic voice that “Elvira” became so closely associated with his baritone, despite his friend Bonsall, a tenor, singing lead.

“I have a voice that is so unusual, when I come out with a low note or a solo part, it’s so different than what the other guys are doing, that it kind of sticks out,” Sterban once said in an interview with Charlie Chase and Lorianne Crook. “It gets a response from the audience and it does make me feel good. Makes me feel like maybe I’m doing something that is right.”

The Country Music Hall of Fame agreed. In 2015, Sterban, along with his Oak Ridge Boys bandmates, was inducted as a member. Just last month, he appeared with some of his Hall of Fame peers during the institution’s Medallion Ceremony in Nashville. Trending Stories ‘SNL’ Cold Open: Jensen Huang, Tech CEOs Get a Crash Course in Female Spies ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs St. Vincent and Metallica Honor Iron Maiden at Rock Hall (With a Jack Black Assist) Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony

In addition to the Country Music Hall of Fame, Sterban, with the Oaks, was also a member of the Gospel Music Hall of Fame — a distinction he shared with his onetime boss, Presley.

“As a young man in my twenties, singing with Elvis, I had no idea that some day I would be in the same Hall of Fame with him. Not only the Country Music Hall of Fame, but the Gospel Hall of Fame as well,” Sterban once told an interviewer. “Very few people can say that.”

#3270. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3269. Foxconn revenue climbs 46%; Bloomberg forecasts 16M iPhone Duo sales

Key Apple manufacturing partner Foxconn has announced a year-on-year revenue increase of 46%, thanks to a mix of consumer electronics and server demand.

Separately, Bloomberg Intelligence has forecast sales of 16 million iPhone Duo units in the first 12 months …

Foxconn is by far the largest contract manufacturer for iPhones, and at one point the majority of its revenue came from Apple. That hasn’t been true for some time, however, largely because of the company’s rapid expansion into servers for AI data centers and cloud storage.

All the same, some 29% of its revenue still comes from its consumer electronics division, of which Apple is by far the largest customer. It’s likely that at least some of its growth comes from the assembly of Apple products.

That’s backed by Bloomberg Intelligence prediction that sales of the iPhone Duo may hit 16 million units by September of next year. That would be well above earlier expectations, with Apple reportedly targeting 9.7M units in the first year before strong demand saw the company raise the goal to 14M.

Bloomberg says that with overall global smartphone demand decreasing due to a difficult economic environment, premium models like the Duo will become increasingly important to Apple’s revenue and profit.

The KitchenAid Artisan Plus has a 5-quart bowl, and comes in an array of colorways.

The Oon Halo Core has a 4.8 quart bowl and comes in either White or Black.

KitchenAid is famous for making some of the best stand mixers on the market. As a home writer who tests a mountain of kitchen appliances, it’s one of the few brands I know I can consistently rely on.

I recently tested one of its newest models, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus, and no surprises, I love it. But straight after giving it a glowing 5-star rating, the Ooni Halo Core spiral stand mixer landed in my kitchen.

While the price tag on both appliances makes my eyes water, I’m wasn't sure what to expect from a brand best known for pizza ovens. Could Ooni really rival KitchenAid? Both are excellent mixers, and I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend them — but which one is the standout winner?

A good benchmark when comparing products is the price. Usually, you can weigh the pros and cons of each appliance and then decide whether the more expensive product is worth the upgrade. But it’s a bit tricky with these two stand mixers, since they hit the same price point — unless you find one on sale.

The KitchenAid Artisan Plus is $599 at Crate & Barrel, although certain colorways are reduced to $429, including Mint Juelp, Steel Blue and Oat.

Ooni’s Halo Core Spiral Dough Mixer is also $599 at Amazon, although it only holds the Foundry Black Colorway. However, you can pick the Polar White colorway directly from Ooni or Williams Sonoma.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

These two mixers are at opposite ends of the spectrum when it comes to design. Ooni offers a much more contemporary style appliance, and its overall aesthetic gives the impression that it means business. It wouldn’t look out of place in a professional kitchen, similar to its big brother, the Halo Pro Spiral stand mixer, which will set you back $799 at Amazon, an extra $200 if you’d prefer the upgrade.

From testing these stand mixers, they both mean business and are sturdy, reliable appliances, but if you’re looking for an appliance to stay out permanently on your countertop, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus would be my choice — though my interior style is more modern cottage than modern urban. And if color is your thing, picking a KitchenAid is a no-brainer!

These mixers both do the same thing—they can beat, whisk and knead —but the Ooni Halo Core is designed with dough in mind. Although it’s still adept at mixing cakes and whisking (it has a double whisk), it really shines at mixing and kneading dough.

While the KitchenAid has a standard dough hook, the Ooni takes it a step further by including a breaker bar. This dual-kneading design develops stronger gluten networks in your dough — perfect if you like to bake homemade pizza in one of Ooni’s pizza ovens. You can see in the above photo how the breaker bar sits centrally in the mixing bowl, and a spiral pattern is made within the dough.

The bowl shield also has a handy feed that ensures that any liquids hit the central point and get quickly incorporated into the mix.

Although both machines can knead a lot of dough, I found the Ooni sat slightly above the KitchenAid in terms of power, but don’t let that put you off buying a KitchenAid if you want to make bread — it’s still an exceptional machine.

The KitchenAid is an excellent all-rounder, and apart from kneading dough without shifting on your countertop, it beats and whips to perfection. I found that the shaped bowl and double flex-edge beater mean that there’s hardly a morsel of cake batter left on the side of the bowl, and you don’t have that annoying problem of having to stop the mix to scrape the sides. You’ll find yourself doing this with the Ooni. For me, the KitchenAid Artisan Plus wins on cakes and pastry, but it doesn’t quite match the Ooni’s speed on dough.

But there is one area where it’s hard to split them. They both have exceptional controls. The KitchenAid uses a sliding scale of 11 speeds, including a slow speed that’s worth using when making powdered-sugar icing. Even a bowl shield can’t protect you from the fine sugary cloud, and this extra slow start is super helpful.

Unlike the KitchenAid, which has numbered levels, the Ooni is based on percentages, and a light illuminates on the speed dial to indicate the setting. What’s more, if you want to pause the appliance, you don’t need to go all the way back to zero; you can just press the control and the machine will pause; press it again, and it will return to the same setting. That’s smart!

I hate to disappoint you after you’ve read through my thoughts on whether the KitchenAid Artisan Plus or the Ooni Halo Core Spiral stand mixer is the better buy, but I can’t declare a single winner.

The truth is, I kept them both. The KitchenAid has taken a permanent spot on my kitchen countertop, while the Ooni sits on a nearby utility shelf.

#3266. The Oak Ridge Boys: 10 Essential Songs

When the Oak Ridge Boys (Duane Allen, William Lee Golden, Joe Bonsall, and Richard Sterban, who died Nov. 14 at 83) were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015, they brought with them some of the most recognizable — and singalong-ready — songs in the genre. From their first hit single, 1977’s “Y’all Come Back Saloon” to their version of “Elvira,” a 1981 crossover smash, the Oaks’ catalog is rich in country music gems. But they also had gospel music in their blood, working heavenly harmonies into secular hits like “Trying to Love Two Women” and releasing full albums of gospel material throughout their decades-long career. Here are 10 of the vocal quartet’s must-hear songs.

The Oak Ridge Boys got their start in the 1940s, when they came out of Knoxville, Tennessee, singing gospel as the Oak Ridge Quintet, and they kept the classic vocal group tradition alive when they went country in the slick 1970s and 1980s. The Oaks’ casual-sharp look and equally pliant musical outlook made their crossover moves feel easy, including appearances on other artists’ tunes (like their beautiful low-key turn on Paul Simon’s “Slip Slidin’ Away”). Their biggest pop moment was “Elvira,” with its jovial gait, horn section, and fun-to-sing hook “Giddy up, um-poppa-um-poppa, mow, mow,” delivered by well-deep bass singer and Camden, New Jersey, native Richard Sterban. (Oaks tenor Joe Bonsall was born just across the Delaware River in Philadelphia.) — J.D.

The Oak Ridge Boys’ 1983 hit warmly celebrated the glories of a homegrown girl by way of comparison with all the foreign goods flooding the American market — from Nikon cameras to blue jeans made in Mexico and French perfume. “From her silky long hair to her sexy long legs/My baby is American Made,” the chorus goes. The song’s trendy protectionist jingoism is delivered with a light touch and goodnatured warmth, so the song never feels mean-spirited, let alone proto-MAGA. It went Number One on the country charts and became an anthem for the band — they even titled their farewell tour after the song. — J.D.

B-b-b-b-building on the success of their recent Number One country and Number Five pop hit “Elvira,” the Oaks stayed lost in that Fifties and Sixties sound and landed another massive crossover hit with “Bobbie Sue,” the title track from their 1982 LP. Penned by Wood Newton with married songwriters Dan and Adele Tyler, “Bobbie Sue” kicks off the tale of “the sweetest grape that ever grew on the vine” with a driving beat reminiscent of “Gimme Gimme Good Lovin’,” the 1969 bubblegum hit by Crazy Elephant, followed by some blazing guitar. Things really pop when Richard Sterban adds his rafter-shaking bass vocal on the stuttering chorus, followed by some stellar accompaniment from the Muscle Shoals Horns. “It’s sort of a 1982 ‘Elvira,’” Joe Bonsall said at the time. Forty-plus years on it’s an underrated pop-country m-m-m-m-masterpiece. — S.L.B.

The Oak Ridge Boys’ second country Number One was a Rodney Crowell rave-up that highlighted everything thrilling about the vocal group: their complex harmonies, interweaving powerhouse vocals, and expert phrasing (listen to the way the group tells the song’s whole story of backwoods freedom by drawing out the word crazy when singing, “If she hadn’t started taking/those crazy chances“). “When I sing ‘Leaving Louisiana (In the Broad Daylight)’ up there with the Oaks, I can think of 1979, man,” Joe Bonsall said, reflecting on the song decades later. “I see us pounding out there on tour with Kenny Rogers, with my hair about four times the size as it is now! It’s a fun thought and a fond memory.” —J.B.

Hey, even the God-fearing Oaks know their way around a cheating song. In this 1980 singalong written by the great Sonny Throckmorton, the band reminds every guy out there that it’s unwise to spread your love too thin. “Trying to love two women is like a ball and chain,” they sang. “Sometimes the pleasure ain’t worth the strain.” William Lee Golden took the lead on this one, with the other three Oaks coming in on that cautionary tale of a chorus. — J.H.

Sharon Vaughn, who in 1976 had a Waylon Jennings cut with the second song she ever wrote, “My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys,” would actually have her first-ever hit single with the first song she ever wrote, the Oak Ridge Boys’ version of “Y’All Come Back Saloon.” A sweet and smoky honky-tonk ballad with just enough church-related references to appeal to the quartet’s gospel roots, the Oaks made the talk-show circuit with the tune just as story-songs like Kenny Rogers’ “Lucille” and “The Gambler” were crossing from country to pop. Although this one didn’t reach as high as the band’s later pop entries, it remained a fan favorite. — S.L.B.

The Oak Ride Boys’ The Boys Are Back included this surprising take on the White Stripes staple, which replaced Jack White’s heavy guitar riffs with layered vocal harmonies. The idea to cover the song came from producer Dave Cobb, who pitched the skeptical group before the band entered the studio. “We get in the studio and [Cobb’s] thinking we’re either crazy and going to kill him or he thinks we’re going to say, ‘Let’s give it a shot.’ And we said, ‘Let’s do it,’” Bonsall told The Tennessean. “Recently we’ve been putting it onstage, and we’re tearing places up with it. It’s just so doggone different.” —J.B.

In July 1973, two months after Joe Bonsall joined the Oak Ridge Boys, Paul Simon featured Black gospel group the Dixie Hummingbirds on his smash hit single “Loves Me Like a Rock.” Simon would revisit gospel music again in 1977, this time with assistance from the Oaks, who had been Simon’s labelmates at Columbia Records before they signed with MCA. Taped in front of an audience of 1,400 at the First Presbyterian Church of Hollywood on Oct. 30, 1986, as part of Cinemax’s Sessions series, this rousing live performance featured Simon on guitar and lead vocal, with the sturdy Oaks backing him up. The harmonies are ethereal. —S.L.B.

The Oaks’ fifth Number One country record spotlights Duane Allen’s lead vocal but relies on the other Boys to add just the right amount of pathos to the sad tale, which finds them “settin’ Fancy free.” But while Fancy might think it’s right to let her go, no one else sounds happy about it. Allen, Bonsall, Golden, and Sterban, however, were sitting on top of the music world, simultaneously watching this song scale the country charts as another woman, “Elvira,” set hearts — and the pop chart — on fire. — S.L.B.

While casual fans may know the Oak Ridge Boys for their country hits, the very roots of the Oaks are gospel songs. In 2018, producer Dave Cobb reconnected the quartet with their hymnbook  stylings on 17th Avenue Revival, a joyous record that celebrated both their heavenly harmonies and their unwavering faith. “Brand New Star,” propelled by vigorous handclaps, acknowledges those who left us for the next life — and it packs an extra emotional wallop in light of Joe Bonsall’s passing. —J.H.

#3264. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3260. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.
