Obviously this is a brand new kind of phone, so it's not like we can look back at previous generations to guess at what might be coming. This makes the S27 Pro a lot more mysterious than the rest of the S27 series. Thankfully, though, the rumors have already started coming, revealing key details about the phone.

Here's everything we know about the Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro so far.

200MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP with 3x optical soom

The Galaxy S27 Pro is rumored to come with a 6.5-inch display, which will sit between the 6.3-inch Galaxy S27 and the 6.7-inch Galaxy S27 Plus. This effectively means that the S27 series will feature a whole range of screen sizes, letting you decide how big your phone wants to be.

While the S27 Ultra is expected to come with Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, leaks claim the Pro will be missing out. Instead it should pack the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the direct successor to the Gen 5 chip that powers most flagship Android phones.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond this we don't know that much about the chip in question, other than the fact it won't be as powerful as the Extreme variant. Presumably Samsung will opt for a custom "for Galaxy" chip that offers more performance power than the standard model, and it's guaranteed to be faster than the Gen 5 chip. But that's all we know for the time being.

It's safe to say that the S27 Pro will have 12GB of RAM, at least on the models with smaller storage variants. RAM costs are through the roof, and Samsung is one of many phone makers that is limiting 16GB of RAM to phones with at least 1TB of storage. That stinks for on-device AI, though it should help keep costs under control.

Like the rest of the S27 series, the Galaxy S27 Pro is expected to come with a triple-lens camera setup. According to database leaks the phone will have the same 200MP main camera lens are the Ultra, paired with a 50MP ultrawide lens and a 10MP telephoto lens capable of 3x optical zoom.

The selfie camera will reportedly user a 16MP sensor, with the Pro and Ultra featuring the same front-facing hardware.

There have been rumors that we could see a 12MP telephoto lens or one with 50MP resolution and 3.5x optical zoom. But considering the Pro model is supposed to be cheaper and less impressive than the Ultra, it makes sense that Samsung would nerf it by repurposing the secondary telephoto lens from the S26 Ultra for an extra year.

Like other Galaxy phones, we know that the Galaxy S27 Pro will have a heavy software focus, though we don't actually know what that might entail. We assume that the phone will run on OneUI 9.5, which is currently in early development, and Galaxy AI will likely play a large role in that update.

Beyond that, we have no idea what changes might be made, or what new software features Samsung will offer. So we'll just have to wait until Galaxy Unpacked to find out, or hope that the details leak between now and January.

Samsung is rumored to be utilizing silicon carbon batteries in the Galaxy S27 series, just as it did with the Z Fold 8 series. This means that the S27 Pro will likely have better battery density, allowing for more power to be squeezed into the same amount of space.

For that reason it's claimed that the S27 Pro will feature a 5,200 mAh battery, which is actually 200mAh more than we saw in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Considering the screen is smaller, and the chip is likely more efficient, it'll be interesting to see how the battery life compares between the two phones.

Charging speed is expected to top out at 60W, with 25W wireless charging. On top of that, rumors claim that the S27 Pro and Ultra will be the only two phones to offer full Qi2 magnetic charging — without needing any special cases.

There's still a lot we don't know about the Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro, and only time can help fill in those gaps. It's likely that more rumors will appear in the coming weeks and months, helping to build a better picture of the phone, but until then we can only speculate as to what this device might have to offer.

That said, it is looking like the S27 Pro will be filling a small niche in the S27 lineup. Acting as a device for those people that want premium features, like high resolution cameras, but don't necessarily want to go overboard on the large (and expensive) Ultra model. It's a bold strategy from Samsung, especially since the S27 is expected to be more expensive than the S26 series, and only time will tell whether it will pay off.

It's all probably going to hinge on how its price compares to the Ultra and Plus models.

#3193. ‘The Gilded Age’ Co-Showrunner Sonja Warfield Reveals How Audra McDonald “Planted The Seed” For “Core Conflict” Of Peggy’s Wedding In Episode 403

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4 Episode 3, titled “Ain’t That Good News.”

Wedding bells are also ringing for the new Dr. (Jordan Donica) and Mrs. William Kirkland (Denée Benton) in The Gilded Age.

The newlywed couple, who met early on in Season 3 of Julian Fellowes’ period drama series, walked down the aisle and officially sealed the deal on their marriage as of Season 4’s third episode, though not without some road bumps along the way.

Elizabeth Kirkland (Phylicia Rashad) takes particular issue with Peggy’s parents gifting their daughter the broomstick they jumped over for their wedding celebration, because Dorothy Scott (Audra McDonald) could not legally marry Arthur Scott (John Douglas Thompson) due to his enslavement. Watch on Deadline

“We were on set filming Season 3, and Audra McDonald turned to me and she said, ‘When they get married next season, I want them to jump over the broom because Elizabeth will hate that,’” co-showrunner Sonja Warfield told Deadline. “And so Audra planted that seed, and so that was going to be their core conflict.”

William’s mother, who hasn’t exactly warmed up to Peggy since the journalist and doctor started their courtship, doesn’t want her son and future daughter-in-law to incorporate the tradition because of its roots in slavery, marking commitment for those in bondage whose unions would not be legally recognized.

“We found out historically that it’s kind of inaccurate. Yes, enslaved people were doing that, but in that time post emancipation, they really weren’t, because then they could legally be married and so the tradition came back really in the 20th century,” Warfield continued. “We got to take some poetic license, artistic license and keep it because we were trying some other things, but really it needed to be that because that represents the division between the families,” Warfield said. “Elizabeth does not want to remember anything from enslavement period, while Peggy wants to pay homage to her family, to her dad and her parents. It is completely like diametrically opposed. So that made for great dramatic conflict.”

Another wrinkle in the plans for the nuptials comes in the form of the Fisk Jubilee singers, led by Dorothy and Peggy’s cousin Ava (Adrienne Warren), who attends Peggy’s pre-wedding tea and announces that she’s brought the choir to sing hymns at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island. Elizabeth is not fond of this idea either, nor, at first, is her husband (Brian Stokes Mitchell), who ultimately presides over Peggy and William’s ceremony. Much like in the show, this addition was not originally in the plans for Season 4’s third episode.

“I believe Sally [Richardson Whitfield] talked to Dr. [Erica] Dunbar because Sally wanted to add more to the wedding, which I was all for. At first, we had to be budget conscious, but then we got some more budget, so then we were able to add the Fisk Jubilee singers,” Warfield said. “I thought it need[ed] to be important to Peggy in a meaningful way, and so then we get to introduce cousin Ava as one of the singers.”

Warfield described the broom as something “tangible” to be angry about regarding Peggy instead of just saying she doesn’t like her soon-to-be daughter-in-law, giving actress Phylicia Rashad plenty of opportunities to “annihilate just with a look.” Meanwhile, the defensiveness Dorothy feels for her daughter is just one of many emotions on the big day.

RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Cast Throughout The Seasons Of The Period Drama

“Dorothy is more than proud; there’s probably everything in it. There’s pride. There’s relief. There’s joy. There’s a little sadness because she has to let go. She’s got to let go in a way that she hasn’t had to. [Dorothy] probably had more time to cling to [Peggy] because of Peggy’s setting out on her own in the beginning, and so all of that is swirled into one,” McDonald told Deadline. “In some ways she starts to feel a little more nostalgic for and a little more romance toward Arthur again. They feel more like a unit now, given how separated they all were in Seasons 1 and 2. So, to see that bond come back together, she’s feeling that, and Peggy is finally getting the joy that she deserves. She’s emerging into this powerful young modern Black woman. That’s a fulfilling thing to see. Her ancestors are definitely smiling down on her.”

“She’s wearing the crown that her ancestors bought and paid for. So that’s a lot of beautiful things come to fruition. In some ways, it may be why Dorothy is so stringent and so unwilling to back down about the broom,” McDonald continued. “That’s honoring the ancestors. Like ‘Yes, you did buy and pay for this crown, and we are honoring you and saying we see you, we thank you, and we give gratitude to and we remember you. That’s why I think Dorothy’s willing to do a knockdown, hat-pulling, hair-pulling fight to get to this moment. That’s why it’s such a beautiful moment when it happens.”

In an interview paired with McDonald, co-star Cynthia Nixon called Peggy’s wedding “the wedding to end all weddings” and she traced the other ceremonies that have speckled The Gilded Age so far.

RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’: How The HBO Drama Created A Castle Fit For A New Duchess

“Every one is different. We’ve had Gladys’s wedding with the bride sobbing down the aisle. We’ve had Enid’s and Oscar’s wedding, which is sort of hilarious. We’ve had Ada and Luke’s wedding, which is late in life and full of anguish because you think Agnes isn’t going to come, and it’s more small and modest,” she said. “The wedding of Peggy and Dr. Kirkland, is this fruition of this tremendous love and the most opulent and beautiful, but also heartfelt and full of tradition and singing and the beautiful attire and the stained glass, and it just it is the apex of all the weddings we’ve ever had on the show.”

McDonald shared one last special association with production behind such a major moment in the show.

“The days that we were shooting it, because it took a long time to shoot, it was the night that the Knicks won. So, we literally had to stop shooting for a while to watch those final moments,” the Tony winner said. “Everybody was stationed at phones and Sally Richardson was like, ‘We can’t keep going. Let’s turn on some TVs.’ And we’re all watching, and then screaming our heads off for I don’t know how late it was. And then we went back to finishing the wedding. We did end up watching the sunrise that night, but it was a worthy night. It was kind of magical that it happened on the night of the of the wedding.”

RELATED: Matt Damon & David Letterman Make Blink & You Missed It Cameos On ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Premiere

#3192. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3190. Opera One for iOS adds Data Saver feature, cutting browsing data usage by up to 80%

Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details.

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active users for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company says can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid plan or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction

Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

#3187. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

Google's new model beats its pricier one and is just as impressive

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google just launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and it could be one of the biggest upgrades to its free AI chatbot yet.

The new model, announced Thursday, is designed to be faster, more accurate and better at following instructions. It even edges out Google's more expensive Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 51 compared with Argon's 50 at Hydrogen's default high reasoning setting.

But the real reason to pay attention is what Hydrogen could mean for everyday Gemini users.

Google says the model is better at handling complicated requests, working with information across different apps and producing useful results without endless follow-up prompts. The company also claims it reduces fabricated information by more than fivefold compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash in its evaluations.

And unlike Google's most powerful Gemini models, Hydrogen is available to free users, although there's a catch. You won't necessarily be able to select it manually without a subscription. Instead, Google's automatic model selection determines when Hydrogen is appropriate for your request.

Here are five ways to put Google's newest AI to work.

Most AI models are good at summarization and pulling out the most important points from documents. But Google says this model in particular can process dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts and other complicated material, pulling relevant details into organized reports and summaries. So, it doesn't only summarize, but it can then implement the information into something you can use. That means you could upload a lengthy insurance policy, school handbook or appliance manual and ask Gemini to find the information you actually need.You can also ask follow-up questions without having to explain the document all over again.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Prompt to try: Read this document and explain the 10 most important things I need to know in plain English. Highlight any deadlines, fees, restrictions or potential problems. Include page references for every important finding and create a table of anything that requires action.

One of the biggest frustrations with AI writing is getting something that sounds natural rather than a generic corporate announcement.

Google says Hydrogen is significantly better at following detailed instructions about tone, length, formatting and style. In theory, that means less time rewriting the same email five different ways.

Try giving it a difficult writing task, such as responding diplomatically to an unreasonable request or explaining something complicated without sounding condescending.The key is giving Gemini specific rules about what you want and what you don't want.

Prompt to try: Help me write a friendly but firm email declining a request. Keep it under 150 words. Make it sound warm, confident and conversational, not overly formal. Avoid corporate jargon, unnecessary apologies and long introductions. Explain my decision clearly and end on a positive note.

This is one of my favorite uses for Hydrogen because it uses the applications you use most within Google Workspace.

Google says the model is better at connecting information from uploaded files, Gmail, Google Drive and supported connected apps, including services such as Dropbox and Airtable. Just keep in mind that you'll need to connect the relevant apps and grant Gemini permission to access them first. Access to individual integrations and actions can also depend on your account and subscription.

Rather than searching through messages individually, you could ask Gemini to piece together information from several sources and turn it into an actionable plan. I've already used it for organizing my busy family schedule and pulling together information for an upcoming project.

Prompt to try: Look through my connected Gmail and Google Drive for information about my upcoming appointments and events over the next two weeks. Create a chronological schedule with dates, times, locations and anything I need to prepare. Flag missing information and tell me which emails or documents contain the details.

Hydrogen isn't just designed to answer questions. Google has also improved its ability to turn plain-English instructions into working interactive projects.

The company demonstrated the model building everything from an interactive 3D globe that visualizes lightning strikes to a virtual island where people can create structures using simple prompts. You don't need to attempt anything nearly that ambitious, but you could ask Gemini to build a household budget calculator, an interactive study guide or a simple game.What I think is cool is what happens after the first version. You can ask Gemini to change colors, add features or fix problems using ordinary language. Keep reiterating to get the best results. In fact, I recommend giving this a try in Gemini's Canvas so you can keep your project organized.

Prompt to try: Create a simple, interactive household budget calculator with fields for monthly income, housing, groceries, utilities, transportation and savings. Automatically calculate the amount remaining after expenses. Include a visual chart and make the design clean, colorful and easy to use on a phone. Show me how to preview and use it.

Hydrogen isn't limited to the Gemini app. Google is also bringing the model to Search, where it says users should see better responses to complicated questions.

Instead of requiring a perfectly worded search, Hydrogen is designed to understand what you're actually trying to accomplish, even when your request includes multiple questions or confusing details.

Google also says its upgraded Search system can discover a wider range of relevant sources and present information in more useful visual formats. The goal is to make Search better at understanding the entire request rather than treating it as a collection of keywords.

Search to try: I need a lightweight laptop for working from coffee shops that has excellent battery life, can handle lots of browser tabs and costs less than $800. Compare my best options, explain the trade-offs and show me reliable reviews.

Head to the Gemini site and sign in with your Google account.

Google is rolling out Hydrogen globally, but the exact experience depends on your subscription. Free users can access Hydrogen through automatic model selection, which chooses the model based on the complexity of the request. Most straightforward questions may still use a lighter model.

If you don't see Hydrogen listed in your model picker, that doesn't necessarily mean you aren't using it. With automatic selection enabled, Google can route appropriate requests to Hydrogen.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen is not Google's most powerful AI model, but I've already experienced what it can do for everyday tasks. Its improvements focus on the things people actually do with AI: understanding documents, writing emails, organizing information, researching purchases and creating useful tools for their life.

Give it a try and let me know in the comments what you think.

#3184. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3183. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3182. Apple TV just debuted three new originals, including a heist thriller series

Up first is “Being Heumann,” which tells the true story of how Judy Heumann led a 1977 protest that resulted in the longest occupation of a federal building in US history.

The movie is directed by Siân Heder, whose previous film, “CODA,” earned Apple its first Academy Award for Best Picture, in addition to winning Best Adapted Screenplay for Heder and Best Supporting Actor for Troy Kotsur.

The premiere of “Being Heumann” also marks the debut of Apple TV’s new sign language accessibility feature, which allows viewers to watch select titles with an American Sign Language (ASL) or British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter appearing in the corner of the screen.

In addition to “Being Heumann,” the feature is also available for “F1 The Movie,” with “Greyhound” and “Way of the Warrior Kid” gaining support later this year. The latter premieres November 25.

The first two episodes of Apple’s anticipated heist thriller series “12 12 12” are now available.

Starring Anthony Mackie (Captain America: Brave New World) and Jamie Dornan (Belfast), the series also features Patrick Fabian (Better Call Saul) and Kali Reis (True Detective: Night Country), among others.

Here’s Apple TV on the new show, which will release new episodes every Friday through December 25:

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

The first of two holiday specials coming to Apple TV this season, “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy” is now also available to stream, the other one being “Fraggle Rock: A Holiday Gift,” which arrives December 4.

The premiere marks the latest release under Apple’s ongoing partnership with Peanuts, and joins a growing collection of original Peanuts productions, alongside classics such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving,” and “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown.”

In fact, “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving” is free to stream on the platform this weekend, meaning even those without an Apple TV subscription can watch it.

Back to “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy,” it follows Snoopy as he tries to get off Santa’s naughty list in the 12 days leading up to Christmas, learning along the way that “there’s more to Christmas than just getting gifts.”

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper is small but mighty, providing a softening top layer to firm beds, despite its 1.5" depth. I slept on a king size topper on top of my medium-firm Plushbeds Botanical Bliss Organic Latex Mattress for a week, and felt immediate added pressure relief across my shoulders, hips and knees. It also helps provide cushioning around my lumbar, preventing a build-up of pain in that area. Plus, its natural materials wick away moisture for breathable sleep. For its $345 queen price, it comes with a 6-month trial run, which is more than most.

Made from natural latex and cotton for breathable sleep

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

As someone who has tested some of the best mattresses and the best mattress toppers you can buy, I can confidently say that the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper is an excellent, naturally cooling choice for softening up firm beds. I slept on a king size Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper on top of my medium-firm Plushbeds Botanical Bliss Organic Latex Mattress for a week and felt an immediate increase in pressure relief across my shoulders, hips and knees.

Type: Natural latexDepth: 1.5 inchesCover: CottonCorner straps: YesTrial period: 180 nightsWarranty: 1-year warrantyStarting MSRP: from $255 (Twin) at Saatva

I've tested some of best Saatva mattresses, and all but one were on the firmer side. It’s no wonder that the brand offers the Saatva Natural Latex Topper because after one week, I’m convinced that it’s the perfect topper to soften up a firm mattress.

Not only is this topper incredibly comfortable and pressure relieving, but it’s supportive enough to sleep on my stomach and back, with enough give to sleep on my side too. Both the natural latex and cotton cover were breathable and kept my temperature neutral throughout the night, so I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty.

On one hand, the 1.5" height won’t require you to buy deeper sheets, however, it may not be thick enough for larger bodies. I should also mention that the topper didn’t quite cover my mattress from one edge to the other. The cover isn’t removeable, and thus washable, but at least it has an antimicrobial treatment to prevent mold and mildew growth.

Overall, I think it’s a solid topper for those who sleep hot or want to soften their firm mattress without making it too soft. Keep reading for my full breakdown of this topper to see if it’s a good choice for you.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper starts out at $255 for a twin size, with a queen priced at $345. The premium price tag is not surprising, considering the topper is made with natural latex. However, we’ve seen more expensive natural latex toppers from Naturepedic ($399 for a queen at full MSRP) and Brooklyn Bedding ($587.07 for a queen on sale) so the Saatva is comparatively excellent value for money.

The price of the Natural Latex Topper includes free shipping, a one-year warranty, and a 180-night sleep trial with free returns.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

We track the best Saatva mattress sales all year round and have never seen this topper on sale, so you don't have to wait for the best time to buy — this is it.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress is 1.5" tall, which is a nice height because I can still use my regular sheets without any issue. Although natural latex is more breathable than memory foam, the perforations in this topper result in even better airflow. The cotton cover helps with breathability and has moisture wicking properties too.

Neither the latex nor the cotton cover is organic, but at least the latex foam is eco-INSTITUT® and Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certified. Saatva also added a Guardin™ botanical antimicrobial treatment which prevents bacteria, mold, and mildew growth. This is a nice perk considering the cover is not removeable.

You can order the topper in any mattress size, but keep in mind that the topper didn’t quite cover my entire king-size mattress. There was about one to two inches of my mattress peeking out on either side of the topper. With the four straps holding the topper in place, I was able to guide it to the center of my mattress.

The only other drawback to the design was the extra fabric that was noticeable when I removed it from the packaging and at the end of testing. I couldn’t feel the fabric sticking up or bunching as I slept, but it’s quite noticeable when the sheets are off the mattress.

I slept on the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper for one week and tested everything from temperature regulation to comfort. Here’s what I found:

Setting the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my bed took five minutes to complete. It arrived vacuum-sealed and rolled up into a small box. The box was pretty damaged but thankfully that did not affect the topper.

Upon removing the plastic, the topper unraveled and expanded. I moved it onto the center of the mattress and noticed that there were a few inches on either side of the mattress, even when it was strapped into place with the corner straps. There was also a lot of extra fabric that bunched up from the cover. The topper had already expanded so I knew right away that the latex wasn’t going to fill out the cover and that for some reason there was just too much fabric.

Memory foam off-gasses and causes smells, but since this topper is made from latex, there were no smells. I slept on the mattress topper that night.

I sleep on an organic natural latex mattress, so when I placed the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my mattress to test, the topper was slightly softer than my mattress. After a week of testing, I’d say the topper offers a medium-soft feel that’s a 5.5 out of 10 on the firmness scale. The surface didn’t contour around my body, and I didn’t sink into the topper. Instead, it provided a hug-like feel, one that relieved pressure across the touch-points of the bed as I slept. My body felt supported and my spine was aligned no matter if I slept on my stomach, back, or side.

I’d suggest using this topper on a firm mattress that’s 7.5 or more out of 10 on the firmness scale, as the topper will provide a more cushioned and comfortable sleep experience, while maintaining the support you need. It could be used on a super soft mattress to extend its life. However, if you're paying $345 to provide extra comfort to a mattress that's lost its support, you could always consider picking up one of the best cheap mattresses instead for around the same price.

I tested the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper in Texas at the end of October and the beginning of November when the temperatures were in the high 70s or low 80s during the day and the low 70s and high 60s at night.

During this time, I turned my air conditioner off and used a fan to sleep at night, though it was still fairly warm in my house (about 70-76 degrees). I didn’t have to worry about overheating because the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper was very breathable and maintained a temperature neutral sleep.

As someone who sleeps on a latex mattress, I expected to have this experience with the topper too, and I was glad to be right. No matter the time of year, I’m confident that the airflow through the perforated latex will ensure a sweat- and heat-free night of sleep.

At first glance, the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper appears to have a 4.7-star rating out of 305 reviews on the Saatva site. However, a closer look shows that all the topper reviews are mixed together, so I wouldn’t trust that rating.

I was able to search the reviews for those who had specifically mentioned buying the Natural Latex Mattress Topper and found reviewers who liked the topper because of its pain-relieving qualities, especially when placed on firmer mattresses.

Because of how the reviews section is designed, it was not easy to find lower-star rating reviews of the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper. Even so, I found a few customers who weren’t fans of the topper, with some stating that the 1.5" thickness flattened too quickly or that the topper developed creases.

✅ Your mattress is too firm: If you love the supportive aspects of a firm mattress but don’t want to wake up with aches and pains, the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper can help. The medium soft feel is comfortable and provides just enough cushioning, while also being supportive.

✅ You overheat at night: The cotton cover and the natural latex work well together to provide a temperature neutral sleep. You won’t get this kind of airflow with a memory foam topper.

✅ You and your partner have different sleep needs: The Saatva Latex Mattress Topper is ideal for any sleep type and those who sleep hot. If your partner likes a firm bed, but you don’t, this topper will provide some cushioning that you need, while maintaining the firm feel your partner likes.

❌ You are trying to firm up your mattress: If you’re trying to provide some more support to your soft mattress or firm it up a bit, the Natural Latex Mattress Topper has too much flexibility.

#3178. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3176. Vanguard Economists Say: Inflation Might Be Better Than It Looks. Here's Why That's Good News for Stocks.

Trump's tariffs haven’t gone away, but their impact on inflation might fade away in 2027.

Inflation has been hanging over the U.S. economy like a cloud. The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data for October 2026 found it increased by 0.4% last month, after rising 0.6% in September.

The current inflation data is nowhere near as bad as it was in 2022, when the inflation rate reached highs over 9%, but it's trending in the wrong direction. Many Americans are feeling pessimistic and worn out from stubbornly high costs of living.

Higher-for-longer inflation motivated the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates by 0.25% at its September meeting. The Fed is also widely expected to raise rates again at its next meeting on Dec. 9, with CME FedWatch forecasting a 90.8% chance of a 25-basis-point hike and a 9.2% chance of a 50-basis-point hike.

Higher interest rates can be bad for stock prices because they raise borrowing costs and reduce the supply of money that's available for investment and economic growth. But recent analysis from Vanguard offers reason for hope.

Let's look at why Vanguard is optimistic about inflation for 2027 -- and what it might mean for your investments.

According to Vanguard, a major driver of inflation in 2026 was the Trump administration's new tariffs in 2025. But those tariffs were technically a one-time price increase; the tariffs don't keep going up every year. That means next year's inflation data might look more encouraging, because any increase in inflation will subtract from a higher base -- the 2026 inflation numbers that already included tariffs.

Vanguard forecasts that core inflation, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, could drop to 2.5% by April 2027. That's close to the Fed's target of 2% and a meaningful improvement from today -- as of September 2026, core inflation was 3.6%.

And Vanguard says this downward move in inflation would come solely from the "tariff roll-off" effect. The tariffs haven't gone away, but they're no longer causing a year-over-year increase in inflation rates. They're already baked into the inflation levels.

Vanguard forecasts a strong year for the U.S. economy in 2027, with 3% GDP growth, 4.4% unemployment, and core inflation of 2.5%. They expect the Fed to hike interest rates one more time in early 2027, bringing the effective federal funds rate to 4.4% (between 4.25% and 4.5%).

If Vanguard's analysis is correct, the U.S. economy could be in great shape in 2027. Inflation doesn't seem poised to become a big economic problem. The tariff effects might fade away. The Fed might not have to raise rates high enough to hurt the job market or cause significant declines in stock prices. The economy might stabilize in a way that's better for consumer prices and, ultimately, better for stock investors.

Vanguard's inflation research didn't make any specific recommendations about stocks or sectors to invest in. But if interest rates don't go much higher in 2027, that could be a bullish sign for tech exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Growth stocks can be more vulnerable to rising interest rates, because investors might move money into high-yield bonds and away from riskier stocks and richly valued sectors. But if inflation and interest rates remain steady or decline in 2027, that could be good news for tech stocks and the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

The Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -1.21%) lets you own 100 of the largest nonfinancial companies on the Nasdaq exchange. It charges a low expense ratio of 0.15%. This fund is similar to the popular Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -1.20%), known as "the Qs."

In the past five years (as of Oct. 31), QQQM has delivered annualized returns of about 13.1% -- including the 2022 bear market and the past few years of rising inflation and interest rates.

What if you're concerned that the AI trade is unsustainable, or you want to diversify and not put too much of your money into tech stocks? The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.38%) might also have a good year in 2027 if inflation and interest rates go in the right direction.

This S&P 500 ETF charges an ultra-low expense ratio of 0.03% and lets you own 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in America. There's some overlap with the stocks in the portfolios of VOO and QQQM. But the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.40%) is less tech-heavy and can put your money to work across a broader range of sectors. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 12% in the past five years (as of Oct. 31).

No matter what happens in 2027 with inflation, interest rates, or the overall economy, investors need to focus on the long term. There's always uncertainty and doubt about the latest alarming news headlines. But in the long run, the stock market tends to deliver strong returns for investors who consistently buy stocks and hold them for many years.

#3174. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

#3172. Security Bite: Apple details Secure Exclaves, a glimpse at its ambient computing future

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.
